3 DECADES
Two particles, linked across
vast distances.
Einstein found the idea
unbearable, and for decades
nobody knew whether he
was right.
In nineteen thirty-five,
Albert Einstein, along
with Boris Podolsky and
Nathan Rosen, argued that
quantum mechanics must
be incomplete, in what
became known as the
EPR Paradox.
They pointed out that
if quantum theory were
true, two particles could
become entangled, linked
so intimately that measuring
one would instantly fix
the state of the
other, however far apart
they were.
Einstein later dismissed
this as spooky action
at a distance,
convinced that it clashed
with the idea that
nothing can influence
anything else faster than
light.
For him, a complete
theory could never allow
such a thing.
For three decades,
the scientific world
remained in philosophical
deadlock.
Did the particles carry
hidden, pre-programmed
instructions given to them
at birth, what physicists
call local hidden variables?
Or was reality fundamentally
nonlocal, interconnected
in a way no
classical picture allows?
In nineteen sixty-four,
a brilliant Northern Irish
physicist named John Stewart
Bell changed the debate
by formulating a
mathematical test: Bell's
Inequality.
Bell proved that if
the classical, commonsense
worldview held by Einstein
were correct, experimental
measurements could never
exceed a strict statistical
limit.
If that limit were
broken, no theory that
was both local and
realistic could be right.
In the early nineteen
eighties, Alain Aspect
carried out landmark
experiments, and
increasingly airtight
loophole-closing tests
followed in later decades.
In twenty twenty-two,
Aspect, John Clauser,
and Anton Zeilinger shared
the Nobel Prize in
Physics for their
experiments with entangled
photons that established
the violation of Bell's
Inequality.
The verdict was clear:
the inequality was violated,
again and again.
Local realism failed the test.
This means either physical
objects do not possess
definite properties prior
to measurement, or distant
particles are linked in
a way no local
mechanism can explain.
Importantly, this link
cannot be used to
send messages faster than
light.
The neat, localized universe
of classical causality
does not describe our world.
Whatever it finally means,
one thing is clear.
The universe is stranger
than classical physics
ever imagined, and
experiments, not opinions,
made that clear.
